scenarios.title: Everyone Starts at Chapter 1
scenarios.situation: A course forces all learners through Chapter 1 regardless of background. Experienced learners disengage from boredom; true beginners are lost by Chapter 3 because gaps were never detected.
scenarios.prompt: What fixes both problems at once?
evidence:
experienced learners: 70% drop by week 2
beginners: 55% fail the midterm
choices: Adaptive placement that maps each learner's prior knowledge and starts them at their own frontier
Keep the linear path but make Chapter 1 skippable on request
Let learners self-place with no assessment
Remove placement entirely - motivation matters more than starting point
scenarios.why: Placement against a knowledge structure puts each learner at their own learnable frontier: experienced learners skip mastered material, beginners get routed to missing prerequisites. Self-placement is unreliable (Dunning-Kruger cuts both ways), and a skippable Chapter 1 still never diagnoses the beginners' gaps.
scenarios.hint: What single mechanism serves the bored expert and the lost beginner simultaneously?

scenarios.title: The All-Nighter
scenarios.situation: A learner has a knowledge check in 7 days. Her plan: re-read the textbook chapter three times the night before. Her last three checks show the same pattern - decent immediately after cramming, failed reassessment two weeks later.
scenarios.prompt: What study plan actually builds durable mastery?
choices: Spaced retrieval practice: short self-testing sessions spread across the 7 days, with reassessment of weak items
Re-read the chapter three times the night before, more carefully this time
Highlight the textbook thoroughly - active marking aids memory
Pull one all-nighter instead of spreading effort - focus beats spacing
scenarios.why: Retrieval practice (testing yourself) strengthens memory far more than re-reading, and spacing the sessions exploits the spacing effect - her own history shows cramming produces fragile, short-lived performance. Highlighting feels productive but barely beats doing nothing.
scenarios.hint: Her history is an experiment with three trials. What did the cramming condition actually produce?

scenarios.title: Failing Percents
scenarios.situation: A learner has failed the 'percents' topic four times. Each failure triggers more percent worksheets, each failed the same way. Her knowledge check shows decimals at 40% and fractions at 55%.
scenarios.prompt: What should the system do next?
evidence: 4 failed attempts at percents; more percent worksheets assigned each time
choices: Route her back to remediate decimals and fractions - percents depend on them
Assign more percent worksheets at higher difficulty
Lower the passing threshold for percents so she can move on
Skip percents and move to the next topic
scenarios.why: Percents sit downstream of decimals and fractions in the prerequisite structure; drilling a downstream topic while its prerequisites are unmastered is futile - the evidence shows the foundation is the gap. Remediating prerequisites is exactly what a knowledge-space model prescribes; lowering the bar or skipping just relocates the failure.
scenarios.hint: Can someone master percents while decimals sit at 40%? Where in the prerequisite chain is the real gap?

scenarios.title: The 50-Question Placement
scenarios.situation: Placement takes every learner through the same fixed 50-question test. Strong learners answer 40 questions far below their level; weak learners suffer through 40 questions far above theirs. Completion rates are falling.
evidence: 'too easy and boring' / 'too hard and humiliating'
choices: Computerized adaptive testing: each response updates the ability estimate and the next item targets that level
Cut the fixed test to 20 random questions
Make the 50 questions untimed to reduce stress
Grade the fixed test on a curve instead
scenarios.why: IRT-based adaptive testing converges on the learner's ability in far fewer items because every question is informative - no floor or ceiling effects, no wasted items. Fewer random questions just add noise; untimed does not fix mis-targeted items; curving re-labels the same bad measurement.
scenarios.hint: What information does a question far above or below your level actually provide? How would you pick the next question?

scenarios.title: Memorizing the Item Bank
scenarios.situation: Learners discover the placement test draws from a small fixed item bank. Scores rise, but proctored reassessments show no real learning - students memorized the specific items and their answers.
evidence: unproctored placement: 85% avg | proctored reassessment: 52% avg
60 fixed items, widely shared among learners
choices: Large calibrated item pools with prerequisite-gated progression - memorizing items cannot fake the underlying knowledge state
Add more items of the same style to the fixed bank
Proctor every assessment heavily
Ignore it - high scores are the goal
scenarios.why: A large pool makes memorizing every item impractical, and prerequisite gating means progress requires the actual knowledge structure, not item recall - the reassessment gap closes because there is nothing to game. More same-style items just expand the cheat sheet; universal proctoring is expensive and treats the symptom.
scenarios.hint: What exactly did the learners memorize - knowledge, or items? Which design makes that distinction irrelevant?

scenarios.title: Where to Set the Bar
scenarios.situation: A course team debates the mastery threshold for advancing: 50% ('don't block learners'), 100% on a single attempt ('true mastery'), or something in between. Dropout and downstream-failure data are on the table.
evidence:
50% threshold -> 60% fail the next module
100% single-attempt -> 45% dropout at the gate
choices: A high bar (around 80-90%) with a reassessment and remediation path - mastery learning's classic compromise
50% - keeping learners moving matters most
100% on a single attempt - anything less is not mastery
No threshold - let learners decide when they are ready
scenarios.why: Bloom's mastery learning sets the bar high (80-90%) but makes time the variable: learners who miss it get diagnosis and retakes instead of permanent failure. The evidence shows 50% passes learners who then fail downstream, while single-attempt 100% converts a learning gate into a dropout machine.
scenarios.hint: What do the two failure modes in the evidence have in common - and what policy avoids both?

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Adaptive Foundations as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Adaptive Learning Foundations Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Adaptive Learning Foundations is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Adaptive Learning Foundations?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Adaptive Learning Foundations issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Adaptive Learning Foundations is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct approach is as follows: Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Adaptive Learning Foundations supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Adaptive Learning Foundations failure in Adaptive Foundations.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Adaptive Learning Foundations
evidence: All Adaptive Learning Foundations components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Start Here: Ground Floor

scenarios.title: Navigate the Bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You have 30 days before your assessment. You open the bootcamp and see 15 domains, a terminal, drills, and a mock. You feel overwhelmed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage first week plan?
choices: Complete Start Here, then work the first three core domains in order — lessons with knowledge checks, then their scenarios, then one lab. Establish the daily loop before widening.
Take the full mock on day one to 'see where you stand,' then study randomly.
Read every lesson in all 15 domains first, then attempt scenarios in week three.
Skip lessons entirely and grind drills — speed matters more than understanding.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is the structured loop: Start Here orients you, then sequential domains build the foundation scenarios assume. The mock on day one wastes your only baseline and demoralizes; random study leaves gaps the assessment will find. Drills without understanding produce fast wrong answers.
scenarios.hint: Think about what the scenarios assume you already know.
evidence: 30 days available, ~2 hours per day on weekdays

scenarios.title: When You Get Stuck
scenarios.situation: You have failed the same scenario three times. The explanation makes sense when you read it, but you keep choosing wrong under time pressure.
choices: Drop back to the lesson: re-read the concepts, write out the decision process in your own words, then re-attempt the scenario untimed before going timed again.
Keep re-attempting the scenario until you memorize the right answer.
Skip it and move on — one scenario will not decide the assessment.
Look up the answer online and move faster through the rest.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats repeated failure as a signal: the mental model is broken, not the memory. Rebuilding from the lesson concepts — in your own words — repairs the model. Memorizing the answer passes one scenario and fails the next variation. The assessment tests patterns, not instances.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem memory or the underlying mental model?
objectives: Repair mental models from lesson concepts
evidence: Scenario failed 3x: same wrong choice twice, different wrong choice once

domains.name: IT Fundamentals

scenarios.title: The Vague Ticket
scenarios.situation: Ticket: 'My computer is broken. Please fix.' No error, no description of what they were doing.
scenarios.prompt: What is your best first move?
choices: Ask what they were trying to do, what they expected, and what actually happened — you need the input and expected output to locate the failing IPO stage.
Remote in immediately and click around to reproduce it.
Reimage the machine — fastest resolution for vague tickets.
Close as 'needs more info' and wait.
scenarios.why: The correct approach completes the IPO picture before acting: input, expected output, actual output. Remoting in blind wastes time, reimaging destroys evidence, and silent closes teach users tickets go nowhere.
scenarios.hint: Which IPO elements are missing from this ticket?
evidence: 'My computer is broken. Please fix.' — no error, no steps

scenarios.title: The 'Missing' Gigabytes
scenarios.situation: User bought a 500 GB drive; Windows shows 465 GB. They suspect a defect or scam.
choices: The drive is probably fine — but verify: check Disk Management for unallocated space first, since a real partition issue is possible.
The drive is defective — start an RMA.
Vendors count decimal GB (1,000,000,000 bytes); Windows counts binary GiB (1,073,741,824). 500B / 1.074B = ~465 — all space present, units differ.
It was mislabeled at the factory.
scenarios.why: The correct approach knows the decimal/binary split (500,000,000,000 / 1,073,741,824 = 465.66) but still verifies with Disk Management — expected behavior explains it, yet a quick check rules out a genuine partition problem before closing the ticket.
scenarios.hint: Who counts in powers of ten vs powers of two?

scenarios.title: The Free Download
scenarios.situation: A colleague installed a 'free' copy of expensive design software from a sketchy site on their work laptop. It works.
choices: Great initiative — share the download source with the team.
Unlicensed software on a company asset: compliance violation, likely malware vector, zero vendor support. Report it, remove it, route a proper license request.
Fine as long as IT doesn't find out.
Only a problem if there's an audit this quarter.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sees legal, security, and operational risk together: unlicensed commercial software plus a cracked installer from an untrusted source is a breach waiting for an audit to discover.
scenarios.hint: What three risk categories apply — legal, security, operational?
evidence: crack-site download; installer flagged by 4 AV engines

scenarios.title: Data vs Information
scenarios.situation: A manager asks for 'all the data' on helpdesk performance. You could dump 50,000 raw ticket rows.
choices: Send the full raw export — they asked for all the data.
Send a 200-slide deck of every chart possible.
Decline — managers should query the database themselves.
Ask what decision it drives, then deliver information: MTTR by category, reopen rate, top recurring issues — processed answers, not raw rows.
scenarios.why: The correct approach converts data to information: raw rows answer nothing alone. Clarifying the decision first prevents building the wrong report.
scenarios.hint: What decision is this data supposed to support?
evidence: 'Send me all the data on helpdesk performance' — no decision stated

scenarios.title: Slow Boot Mystery
scenarios.situation: PC takes 12 minutes to boot. Task Manager shows disk at 100%, CPU idle, RAM half-used during boot.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the bottleneck and the fix?
choices: Disk I/O: a spinning HDD thrashing at 100% while CPU idles is the textbook I/O bottleneck. Migrate to SSD — RAM/CPU upgrades can't help idle resources.
CPU is too slow — replace it.
Add more RAM — RAM is always the answer.
Reinstall Windows — clean slate fixes everything.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the saturated resource: disk at 100% with idle CPU means the system waits on I/O. Fix the binding constraint — an SSD removes it.
scenarios.hint: Which resource is saturated, which are idle?

scenarios.title: The Corrupted File
scenarios.situation: A critical spreadsheet opens as garbage. File size looks normal; it was fine yesterday.
scenarios.prompt: Most likely cause, and first step?
choices: Permanently destroyed — tell the user to rebuild it.
Definitely malware — full antivirus scan immediately.
Bit-level corruption or app mismatch — first check backups/previous versions before touching it, then try another app to separate file damage from app damage.
The hard drive is failing — replace it now.
scenarios.why: The correct approach protects recoverability first: version history exists for this moment, and a second app distinguishes file damage from application damage. Skipping cheap checks wastes the easy wins.
scenarios.hint: What separates a damaged file from a damaged application?

scenarios.title: The Unopenable Attachment
scenarios.situation: A client sent a .pages document; nobody on the Windows team can open it. The deadline is in two hours.
choices: Ask the client to retype the content into an email.

Ask the client to export as PDF or .docx and resend — the format belongs to one vendor's app; converting at the source preserves fidelity. Meanwhile try an online converter as a stopgap, never for sensitive content.
Screenshot each page from a Mac-owning friend.
Rename it to .docx — extensions are just hints.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the format as the problem, not the file: .pages needs Apple's app, so source-side export is the fidelity-safe fix. Renaming never converts bytes; screenshots destroy quality.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem the file or the format?

domains.name: Networking Basics

scenarios.title: The Website That Would Not Load
scenarios.situation: Whole office can't reach the intranet site; external sites work. Intranet IP pings; its hostname doesn't resolve.
choices: The internet connection is down.
The intranet web server crashed.
Internal DNS: IP works but the name fails while external names work — the resolver lacks the internal zone. Check client DNS settings and internal zone records.
The firewall blocks the intranet.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates resolution from connectivity: working IP + failing name + working external names isolates the fault to internal DNS records or the internal resolver view.
scenarios.hint: IP works, name fails — which service translates names?

scenarios.title: The Duplicate Address
scenarios.situation: Two users drop intermittently at different times; rebooting briefly fixes it. Both show 192.168.1.44.
choices: IP conflict: two devices hold one address (likely a static inside the DHCP pool). Find the static, move it outside the pool or make a reservation.
The switch is failing — replace it.
Both NICs are dying at once.
The DHCP server is down.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes the signature: identical IPs plus intermittent drops is a conflict; rebooting only helps until the other machine reasserts. Permanent fix is addressing hygiene.
scenarios.hint: Same IP twice + intermittent drops = ?

scenarios.title: Timed Out vs Refused
scenarios.situation: Monitoring can't reach an agent on port 5666: 'connection timed out.' The agent is confirmed running and listening.
scenarios.prompt: What does the timeout tell you? Next step?
choices: The agent is misconfigured — reinstall it.
Timeout and refused are the same — reboot the target.
The cable is unplugged.
Silently dropped packets = a firewall in the path (refused would mean nothing listening). Check host and network firewall rules for TCP 5666.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the error: a running service plus silence means a filter drops the SYNs. Check the firewall rules for that port — reinstalling a running service fixes nothing.
scenarios.hint: Silence vs active refusal — what does each mean?

scenarios.title: The Wrong Subnet
scenarios.situation: Printer at 192.168.5.20/24 unreachable from 192.168.1.0/24 workstations; pings fine from 192.168.5.50.
choices: The printer is broken — replace it.
Different subnets (/24: third octet must match) with no routing between them. Move the printer to the workstation subnet or add routing.
Workstations need new NICs.
Printers can't work across IP addresses.
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies the mask: the laptop test proves the printer is healthy, so the fault is topology — re-address or route.
scenarios.hint: Under /24, which octets must match?

scenarios.title: Worked Yesterday, Dead Today
scenarios.situation: Conference PC worked yesterday; today ipconfig shows 169.254.x.x. Neighbors on the same switch work.
choices: APIPA: DHCP unreachable, so the PC self-assigned link-local. Server and uplink are fine (neighbors work) — check this PC's cable/port, then release/renew.
Virus — quarantine the PC.
169.254 is normal — the internet is down.
Reinstall the OS.
scenarios.why: The correct approach knows APIPA signals DHCP failure, and working neighbors isolate it to this PC's physical path or NIC. Fix the path, then renew.
scenarios.hint: What does 169.254 prove about DHCP?

scenarios.title: The Slow Application
scenarios.situation: Cloud app is 'slow.' tracert: hops 1-3 <2ms, hop 4 jumps to 280ms sustained to destination.
choices: Your router is failing — replace hop 1.
Traceroute is unreliable — reboot everything.
Latency enters at hop 4 — past your LAN, at the ISP/peering handoff. Local network is clean; escalate upstream with the traceroute as evidence.
The app server needs more CPU.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the latency step: a sustained jump at a boundary past your network means the delay isn't yours to fix locally — it's escalation evidence pinpointing where to look.
scenarios.hint: Where does latency first appear?

scenarios.title: Full Bars, No Internet
scenarios.situation: A user reports 'the Wi-Fi is down' — full signal bars, but nothing loads. Their phone on the same Wi-Fi works fine.
choices: The router needs rebooting.
The wireless access point has failed.
The ISP is down.
The user's device: Wi-Fi radio works (bars = signal), so isolate per-device — check its IP/DNS (APIPA? wrong DNS?), forget and rejoin the network, compare with the working phone.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates signal from service and per-device from infrastructure: full bars plus a working phone means the AP and uplink are fine — the fault lives in this device's network config. Rebooting the router would disrupt everyone for one device's problem.
scenarios.hint: Bars measure signal, not internet — and one working device changes the scope. What's left?

domains.name: OS Fundamentals

scenarios.title: Access Denied
scenarios.situation: User can open but not save to the department share. A colleague in the same department edits fine.
choices: The file server is out of disk space.
Permissions: user missing from the write group or hit by a deny ACE. Check Effective Access for that user — it computes share + NTFS + group nesting into one answer.
User's password expired.
Loose network cable.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses the working peer to eliminate server/share/network, isolating the fault to this user's effective permissions — which Effective Access resolves directly.
scenarios.hint: A peer works — what does that eliminate?
evidence: Read OK, write denied — one user

scenarios.title: The Frozen App
scenarios.situation: Spreadsheet app freezes daily ~3 PM; reboot fixes until next day. Window won't close.
choices: App is corrupt — reinstall immediately.
User needs a new computer.
Tell them to avoid spreadsheets at 3 PM.

Check Task Manager at 3 PM: app CPU/disk plus child processes. A daily pattern suggests a scheduled trigger (auto-save to slow share, add-in, backup lock). Kill the process tree; investigate the trigger.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the time pattern as the prime clue: same-hour recurrence points at a scheduled event interacting with the app. Resource readings separate 'working hard' from 'wedged waiting.'
scenarios.hint: What does a strict daily pattern suggest?

scenarios.title: The Full Disk
scenarios.situation: Server alerts C: at 98%, up 40 GB in a week. App team says 'just add disk.'
choices: Find what's growing: runaway logs, temp, stuck backup. 40 GB/week has a cause — more disk only delays the next alert while hiding it.
Add disk immediately.
Delete oldest files.
Reboot to clear temp.
scenarios.why: The correct approach diagnoses before expanding: sudden growth is a symptom with a cause. Pinpoint with disk-usage tools, then fix the source.
scenarios.hint: What does 40 GB in a week say about 'just add disk'?

scenarios.title: The Service That Will Not Stay Up
scenarios.situation: Critical service stops every few hours; manual start works temporarily. App logs show nothing.
choices: Reinstall the app — binaries must be corrupt.
Server needs more RAM.

System event log + service config: dependency failures, expired service-account passwords, and resource exhaustion are the classic 'runs then dies' causes — the Service Control Manager logs each stop with a reason.
Disable the firewall.
scenarios.why: The correct approach goes to OS-level truth: SCM records why it stopped a service, with reason codes the app log never sees. Evidence before reinstall.
scenarios.hint: Who manages service lifecycle and what does it log?

scenarios.title: The Linux Permission Denied
scenarios.situation: Backup script runs on Windows but on Linux: 'Permission denied.' The admin can read the file.
choices: Linux can't run backup scripts.
Missing execute bit: Linux needs x to run a file, independent of read. chmod +x — then check the shebang and line endings, the other cross-platform paper cuts.
File corrupted in transfer.
Must log in as root.
scenarios.why: The correct approach knows read and execute are separate bits. Shebang + CRLF checks cover the next most common Windows-to-Linux script failures.
scenarios.hint: Which bit does execution require?

scenarios.title: The Update That Broke Things
scenarios.situation: After patching, three app servers can't reach the healthy, patched DB server.
scenarios.prompt: Likely cause category and first check?
choices: Patches defective — roll back everything now.
DB is lying about health.
Network team broke something.
A patch changed a default: firewall rules reset, TLS tightened, service behavior changed. Diff firewall rules and service state vs pre-patch baseline; test per layer.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats post-change breakage as change-caused until proven otherwise. Patches routinely reset firewall profiles — find the specific change before rolling back blindly.
scenarios.hint: First question when breakage follows a change?

scenarios.title: The Ransomware Morning
scenarios.situation: A user's files are encrypted with a ransom note. The PC also holds the only copy of the team's shared project folder — synced from their local drive, now encrypted too, and the sync pushed it to the 'cloud.'
scenarios.prompt: What's the recovery play, and what failed?
choices: Pay the ransom — it's the only way.
Wipe the PC and accept the data loss.

Isolate the PC from the network immediately; restore the project from a versioned/offline backup (sync is not backup — it faithfully copied the encryption). The failure: no 3-2-1 backup and sync mistaken for backup.
Restore from the sync cloud folder — it has the files.
scenarios.why: The correct approach isolates first to stop spread, then restores from a real backup — and recognizes the sync service propagated the damage, which is exactly why sync is not backup. Paying funds crime with no guarantee.
scenarios.hint: Did the 'cloud copy' protect anything here? Why not?
evidence: Cloud folder shows encrypted versions, synced 06:12

scenarios.situation: You are about to start the Documented Home Lab capstone. You have limited lab time and want maximum interview value.
scenarios.prompt: How do you scope the build?
choices: Write the plan first: phases with definitions of done, mapped to bootcamp domains. Start with the smallest working core, then layer on complexity. Document decisions as you go.
Start building immediately — planning wastes lab time.
Attempt the most impressive architecture possible to stand out.
Build whatever is easiest to finish quickly.
scenarios.why: The correct approach balances ambition with completion: a planned, phased build that finishes is worth more than an impressive unfinished one. Mapping phases to domains turns the capstone into applied review of the whole course.
scenarios.hint: What does the interviewer actually evaluate in a project?

domains.name: Hardware Basics

scenarios.title: Dead on Arrival
scenarios.situation: Desktop shows zero signs of life: no fans, no lights, no beeps. Worked last week; thunderstorm Friday.
choices: Replace the motherboard immediately.
Reinstall Windows.
Replace the CPU.
Outlet/cable, then PSU switch and connections, then known-good PSU or tester — no signs of life means no power reaching the board; start at the wall, move inward.
scenarios.why: The correct approach follows the power path inward: wall -> cable -> PSU -> board. No signs of life is power delivery; replacing boards or CPUs skips cheaper, likelier culprits.
scenarios.hint: What does 'no signs of life at all' rule out?
evidence: No fans, no LEDs, no beeps

scenarios.title: The Beep Code
scenarios.situation: PC powers on, fans spin, no display. Three long beeps repeating; manual says 3 beeps = memory error.
choices: Replace the graphics card.
Power off, reseat the RAM (remove, clean contacts, firmly reinsert), test one stick at a time in the primary slot — beep codes name the subsystem; reseat before replacing.
Update the BIOS.
Buy a new PC — beeps mean it's dead.
scenarios.why: The correct approach trusts the diagnostic: the board identified memory, so work the memory — reseat, isolate sticks, try slots. Replacing the GPU ignores what the machine told you.
scenarios.hint: The motherboard already diagnosed it — what's your job now?

scenarios.title: The Aging Laptop
scenarios.situation: Six-year-old laptop, HDD, 10 minutes to usable. CPU/RAM modest but adequate. Tight budget.
choices: Add more RAM first.
Replace the CPU.
Migrate to an SSD: on HDD-era machines the disk is the binding constraint for boot and launch — a $40 SSD transforms usability more than any other single upgrade.
Buy a new laptop.
scenarios.why: The correct approach targets the bottleneck: HDD latency dominates boot/app-launch on old laptops. SSD migration is the cheapest transformation available.
scenarios.hint: Which component caps boot and launch here?

scenarios.title: The Mystery Shutdowns
scenarios.situation: Workstation shuts off hard (instant black) during heavy renders, restarts fine, dies again under load. Kernel-Power 41.
choices: Thermal shutdown or PSU overload: instant-off under load is the signature of heat protection or power starvation. Check CPU/GPU temps and fans first, then PSU wattage vs load.
Windows is corrupt — reinstall.
The render software has a bug.
RAM is failing.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the signature: hard-off under load (not bluescreen, not app crash) means protection circuitry fired — heat or power. Temps and PSU math before software theories.
scenarios.hint: Hard power-off under load vs bluescreen — what does each indicate?

scenarios.title: The Clicking Drive
scenarios.situation: HDD clicking; SMART reallocated sectors climbing. No backup exists.
choices: Run a full surface scan to map bad sectors.
Defragment to stabilize it.
Tell the user clicking is normal — keep working.
Image/back up the data FIRST — a clicking drive with growing reallocations is actively dying; every spin risks more loss. Then replace the drive.
scenarios.why: The correct approach puts data before diagnosis: remaining life is measured in hours, and scans/defrags stress the drive further. Image first, replace, then investigate.
scenarios.hint: What is irreplaceable — the drive or the data?

scenarios.title: The Intermittent Gremlin
scenarios.situation: PC randomly freezes — hourly or fine for days. Drivers current, OS healthy, temps normal.
choices: Reinstall Windows again.

Minimal-boot isolation plus overnight MemTest86: intermittent freezes with healthy software/temps point at marginal RAM or power. Strip to board + CPU + 1 RAM stick, test, add parts back one at a time.
Replace the motherboard.
Blame the user.
scenarios.why: The correct approach isolates instead of guessing: software and thermals cleared leaves marginal hardware, and minimal-boot plus memory testing finds it systematically. Another reinstall changes nothing proven healthy.
scenarios.hint: Software and heat are cleared — what cause class remains?
evidence: Random freezes, hours to days apart

scenarios.title: The Phantom Printer
scenarios.situation: User's printer shows 'Offline' but it's powered on and was working yesterday. Three other users print to it fine.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the fault, and first check?
choices: The printer's network card is dying.
The print server is down.
On the user's machine: their queue has a stuck job or a stale port. Clear the queue, verify the port/IP matches the printer's current address (DHCP may have moved it), then re-add if needed.
Replace the printer.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses the working users to eliminate the printer and server, isolating the fault to this client's queue or port config. A DHCP address change breaks the mapped port silently — the classic 'worked yesterday' printer fault.
scenarios.hint: Others print fine — what does that eliminate?

domains.description: The physical layer: CPU/RAM/storage, power and connectivity, the boot process, isolation troubleshooting, and peripherals.

domains.name: Security Awareness

scenarios.title: The Urgent Invoice
scenarios.situation: Email from 'CEO' (display name) demands an urgent wire transfer, reply-to is a Gmail address, link hovers to a misspelled domain.
choices: Don't click or reply: verify via a known channel (call the CEO's known number), report to IT/security with headers. Urgency + mismatched sender + lookalike domain = textbook spear phishing.
Reply asking for confirmation — the CEO will clarify.
Click the link to see if it's legitimate.
Forward to colleagues to warn them, then delete.
scenarios.why: The correct approach verifies through a second channel and reports: display names lie, reply-tos redirect, and urgency is the weapon. Clicking 'to check' executes the attack; forwarding spreads it.
scenarios.hint: What three tells are in this email?

scenarios.title: The Reused Password
scenarios.situation: A breach dump includes a user's email + password. They reuse that password on their work VPN and personal banking.
choices: Only change the breached site's password.
Delete the breach notification email.
Wait to see if anything happens.
Change the password everywhere it's reused — work VPN and banking FIRST (email is the reset master key), enable MFA, then use a password manager to make every password unique going forward.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats credential stuffing as already underway: attackers automate reuse within hours. Priority is the accounts that unlock others (email, VPN, banking), then uniqueness everywhere via a manager.
scenarios.hint: Which accounts unlock all the others?
evidence: Same password on VPN and banking

scenarios.title: The Free Game Cheat
scenarios.situation: A user's kid installed a 'free game cheat' on the work laptop. Now pop-ups flood the screen and the AV is disabled.
choices: Re-enable the AV and keep working.

Disconnect from the network immediately, report to IT with the timeline, don't enter credentials — the machine is compromised (trojan with AV-killer behavior). Scan from clean media or reimage; investigate how it got on a work device.
Run a quick AV scan while continuing to work.
Let the kid finish the game, then uninstall it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach contains first: disabled AV plus pop-ups after a cheat install is active compromise. Continuing to work or just re-enabling AV leaves persistence mechanisms in place; the device and the policy gap both need attention.
scenarios.hint: What does disabled AV after a cheat install indicate?
evidence: 'Free cheat' installed by family member on work laptop

scenarios.title: The Parking Lot USB
scenarios.situation: An unlabeled USB drive is found in the company parking lot. A curious employee wants to plug it in to find the owner.
choices: Plug it into a work machine to check for owner files.
Plug it into a personal phone instead — safer.
Hand it to IT/security unplugged: found media is a classic attack vector (malicious autorun/fake files). Never plug in unknown media; IT can inspect it safely if needed.
Throw it in the trash.
scenarios.why: The correct approach never trusts found media: USB attacks (BadUSB, malicious LNK files) execute on insertion, and 'safer' devices are still vulnerable. IT handles it — curiosity is the exploit.
scenarios.hint: What executes when you plug in a malicious USB?

scenarios.title: The 2 AM Alert
scenarios.situation: EDR alerts: a server is beaconing to an unknown external IP at 2 AM. No approved change is scheduled.
choices: Isolate the host from the network (keep it powered), escalate to security with the alert details and timeline, preserve logs — beaconing off-hours with no change window is a compromise indicator until proven otherwise.
Delete the alert to keep the dashboard clean.
Wait until morning — probably a false positive.
Reboot the server to clear it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats unexplained beaconing as compromise: isolate to stop exfiltration/lateral movement, preserve state for forensics (don't reboot away memory evidence), and escalate with the timeline.
scenarios.hint: What does unexplained off-hours beaconing suggest?

scenarios.title: The MFA Fatigue Attack
scenarios.situation: A user gets 20 MFA push notifications at midnight they didn't request. They approve one 'to make it stop.'
scenarios.prompt: What just happened, and the fix?
choices: The user should approve faster next time.
MFA is broken — disable it.
The MFA system is glitching — restart the phone.

Attackers with the user's password are spamming push approvals hoping for one tired tap (MFA fatigue). Deny all, change the password from a clean device, report to security, switch to number-matching or a security key.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes push-bombing: the attacker already has the password and needs one approval. The tap granted access — so rotate credentials, review sessions, and move to phishing-resistant MFA.
scenarios.hint: Why would an attacker send pushes the user didn't request?

scenarios.title: The Airport Wi-Fi
scenarios.situation: At an airport, a user joins 'Free Airport WiFi' (no password) and logs into the company VPN and webmail without a VPN client running.
scenarios.prompt: What are the risks and the correct habit?
choices: No risk — the Wi-Fi name looks official.

Open Wi-Fi exposes unencrypted traffic to anyone nearby (evil-twin APs, sniffing). Habit: phone hotspot preferred; on open Wi-Fi use the company VPN before anything, HTTPS only, forget the network after.
Only risk is slow speed.
The VPN login was the mistake — don't use VPNs on public Wi-Fi.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats open networks as hostile: names are spoofable, traffic is sniffable. The company VPN encrypts the tunnel — the fix is using it first, not avoiding it.
scenarios.hint: Can you trust a network name? What protects traffic on hostile networks?
evidence: VPN + webmail login, no client VPN

domains.description: Think like a defender: the CIA triad, phishing, passwords and MFA, malware, and staying safe on any network.

domains.name: Cloud Concepts

scenarios.title: Which Cloud Model?
scenarios.situation: A startup wants to launch a web app fast with two developers and no ops staff. They need a database, app hosting, and email.
choices: IaaS for everything — maximum control.
On-premises servers — cheapest long-term.
PaaS for the app + database (provider manages the stack), SaaS for email — two developers ship product instead of babysitting servers; ops burden outsourced where it adds no value.
Build their own data center.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches the model to the team's scarcest resource (ops time): PaaS removes server management, SaaS removes email ops entirely. IaaS would buy control they can't staff.
scenarios.hint: What is this team's scarcest resource?

scenarios.title: The Open Bucket
scenarios.situation: A company's cloud storage bucket with customer data is found publicly readable. The provider's service worked exactly as designed.
scenarios.prompt: Who is responsible, and the systemic fix?
choices: No one — it was a hack.
The customer: shared responsibility puts data and configuration on you. Fix: default-deny bucket policies, automated config auditing, and alerts on public exposure.
The customer who uploaded the data.
The cloud provider — their service allowed it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies shared responsibility: the provider secures the service, you secure your configuration. 'Worked as designed' is the tell — the design obeyed your public setting.
scenarios.hint: The service worked as designed — so whose design choice failed?

scenarios.title: The Surprise Bill
scenarios.situation: A dev team's monthly cloud bill jumps from $800 to $9,000. Nobody changed the architecture knowingly.
choices: Top services by cost, then idle/unattached resources, then egress/cross-region transfer, then untagged sprawl. Common culprits: forgotten load-test rigs, unattached disks, a runaway auto-scaler.
Delete everything and start over.
Blame the provider's pricing.
Pay it and move on — cloud is just expensive.
scenarios.why: The correct approach triages the bill like an incident: biggest line items first, then the classic waste patterns. Bill shocks are almost always forgotten resources or runaway automation, not price changes.
scenarios.hint: Where does cloud waste hide?

scenarios.title: The Latency Complaint
scenarios.situation: EU users complain the app is slow; US users are fine. All infrastructure sits in one US region.
scenarios.prompt: Fix that respects physics and law?
choices: Add more US servers.
Tell EU users to get faster internet.
Compress all images more.
Serve EU from an EU region (or CDN edge): latency follows distance, and EU data may legally need EU residency. Multi-region or edge caching fixes both physics and compliance.
scenarios.why: The correct approach respects physics (round-trips across the Atlantic can't beat light speed) and law (data residency). Edge/CDN or an EU region addresses both; more US servers fixes neither.
scenarios.hint: What can't be optimized away — distance or code?

scenarios.title: The SaaS Breach
scenarios.situation: A SaaS CRM is breached via a former employee's still-active login. The SaaS provider's infrastructure was not compromised.
choices: The SaaS provider's fault — demand compensation.
Unpatchable — accept the risk.
Identity lifecycle failure on the customer side: deprovisioning didn't revoke the SaaS account. Fix: tie SaaS to SSO with automated deprovisioning on termination; audit seats quarterly.
The ex-employee's fault alone.
scenarios.why: The correct approach puts it on the customer's half of shared responsibility: SaaS identity lifecycle is yours. SSO + automated deprovisioning closes the joiner-mover-leaver gap permanently.
scenarios.hint: Whose half of shared responsibility covers user accounts?

scenarios.title: The Migration Plan
scenarios.situation: A company must move 40 legacy apps to cloud in 9 months. Half are stable and rarely change; a few are under active development.
choices: Big-bang cutover in month 9.
Wave it: rehost the stable apps fast (keep the debt, hit the date), replatform/refactor the active ones where payoff justifies it, retire anything unused. Migrate by dependency order with rollbacks.
Move the hardest app first alone.
Rewrite all 40 cloud-native — do it right.
scenarios.why: The correct approach differentiates by workload: stable apps earn lift-and-shift (speed), active ones earn deeper work (payoff), dead ones earn retirement. Waves with rollbacks beat big-bang heroics.
scenarios.hint: Do all 40 apps deserve the same strategy?

scenarios.title: The Wildcard IAM Policy
scenarios.situation: An audit finds a cloud IAM policy granting *:* (all actions, all resources) to a developer role used by 30 people.
choices: Any compromised credential in that role = full cloud takeover. Fix: scope to least privilege (specific actions on specific resources), require MFA, review with access advisor data.
Delete the role entirely.
It's fine if the developers are trustworthy.
Convenient — leave it; developers need access.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats *:* as the keys to the kingdom: one phished developer credential becomes total compromise. Least privilege isn't bureaucracy — it's blast-radius control.
scenarios.hint: What does one compromised credential unlock here?

domains.description: The cloud without the hype: service models, regions and zones, shared responsibility, costs, and migration strategies.

domains.name: Data Literacy

scenarios.title: The Shared Workbook Nightmare
scenarios.situation: Five people edit 'the master tracker' spreadsheet. Versions multiply, rows vanish, and nobody knows which copy is current.
choices: Lock the spreadsheet with a password.
Move it to a database (or a proper tracker tool) with concurrent access, audit history, and backups — the pain is the crossover signal. Keep a spreadsheet as the analysis view if needed.
Email it around less often.
Assign one person to merge copies weekly.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes the crossover: multi-editor + integrity needs = database territory. Passwords and merge rituals treat symptoms; concurrent systems with history fix the structure.
scenarios.hint: Which crossover triggers are present here?

scenarios.title: The Report Request
scenarios.situation: Manager: 'Which product categories grew fastest last quarter?' Data lives in an orders table (product, category, amount, date).
choices: SELECT category, SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE date in last quarter GROUP BY category, compare to prior quarter — filter, group, aggregate: the reporting shape.
Ask IT to build a dashboard first.
SELECT * FROM orders — then eyeball it.
Download everything and pivot by hand.
scenarios.why: The correct approach thinks in SQL before tools: filter the period, group by category, aggregate revenue. The shape is the same whether you write SQL, a pivot table, or a BI tool.
scenarios.hint: Filter? Group? Aggregate?

scenarios.title: The Duplicate Customers
scenarios.situation: Marketing's campaign mailed 3 catalogs to the same household. The customer table has 'Jon Smith', 'John Smith', 'J. Smith' — same address.
choices: Mail less often.
Deduplicate once by hand.
Validate at entry: standardized name/address fields, duplicate detection on the key (address + name fuzzy match), and a merge process — cleaning once without entry controls guarantees recurrence.
Blame data entry staff.
scenarios.why: The correct approach fixes the source, not the instance: entry-time validation and dedup keys prevent recurrence. One manual cleanup without controls is mopping with the tap running.
scenarios.hint: Why will one cleanup not stick?

scenarios.title: The Dramatic Chart
scenarios.situation: A vendor's chart shows their product 'crushing' competitors: bars from 94% to 98%, y-axis starting at 90%.
choices: Charts don't lie.
Buy their product.
Impressive — 4 points is a big lead.
The axis starts at 90%, inflating a 4-point gap into a visual landslide. Real difference is small; also ask about sample, methodology, and who funded the chart.
scenarios.why: The correct approach checks the axis first: truncated axes are the oldest trick in chart persuasion. A 4-point gap on a 0-100 scale is a sliver, not a landslide.
scenarios.hint: Where does the y-axis start, and what does that do visually?

scenarios.title: The Wrong Container
scenarios.situation: A team stores 2 million sensor readings per day in a shared spreadsheet. It's 800 MB, crashes on open, and two analysts need it simultaneously.
choices: A bigger spreadsheet app.
A time-series database (or any real database): built for high-volume appends, concurrent readers, and range queries. The spreadsheet was the wrong container two million rows ago.
Split into 365 yearly spreadsheets.
Email CSVs around instead.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches container to shape and scale: append-heavy time-series data with concurrent readers is textbook database territory. Splitting spreadsheets multiplies the chaos.
scenarios.hint: What shape is this data, and what breaks at this scale?

scenarios.title: The Critical Spreadsheet
scenarios.situation: The finance team's budget model lives in one spreadsheet on one laptop. No backup. The laptop is 5 years old.
choices: Single copy on aging hardware = single point of failure for the company's budget. Immediate: copy to shared/cloud storage with versioning; then treat it as production data with backups.
Buy a new laptop.
Print it out.
It's fine — laptops are reliable.
scenarios.why: The correct approach names the risk plainly: unbacked production data on old hardware. Versioned cloud/shared copies are the fast fix; the deeper fix is recognizing the spreadsheet as production data.
scenarios.hint: How many copies exist? How many failures from loss?

scenarios.title: The Misleading Average
scenarios.situation: 'Average user session is 45 minutes!' But the median is 4 minutes — a few marathon sessions skew the mean.
choices: Stop measuring sessions.
The average is fine — 45 minutes sounds great.
Report the median (4 min) and the distribution: the mean is dragged by outliers. Show both, explain the skew, and segment (what do marathon users do differently?).
Delete the marathon sessions as errors.
scenarios.why: The correct approach distrusts the lonely average: with skew, the median describes the typical user. Showing the distribution turns a misleading headline into an insight about power users.
scenarios.hint: What does mean-vs-median divergence tell you?

domains.description: Work with data confidently: types, databases vs spreadsheets, SQL thinking, data quality, and honest charts.

domains.name: Automation Intro

scenarios.title: Automate or Endure?
scenarios.situation: A tech spends 30 minutes every Monday compiling a status report by hand from three systems. It's error-prone and dreaded.
choices: Hire an intern to do it.
Stop sending the report.
Keep doing it manually — automation is risky.
Automate: 30 min/week = 26 hours/year of dread plus errors. A few hours of scripting pays back in weeks; start read-only (pull the data, draft the report) and keep a human review step.
scenarios.why: The correct approach runs the ROI: high frequency x real time x error cost = clear automation win. Read-only first with human review keeps risk low while capturing most of the value.
scenarios.hint: Frequency x time x error cost = ?

scenarios.title: Automating the Mess
scenarios.situation: A team wants to script their server provisioning — but the manual process is undocumented, varies per admin, and half the steps are tribal knowledge.
choices: Write the script now — automation will force standardization.
Buy an automation platform first.
Document and standardize the manual process first: automation multiplies whatever it touches — codifying chaos produces fast, consistent chaos. Script the stable process second.
Automate only the easy parts.
scenarios.why: The correct approach fixes the process before the tooling: scripts amplify — a standardized process becomes reliable automation, a tribal one becomes reliable breakage. Tools don't create order.
scenarios.hint: What does automation multiply?

scenarios.title: The Silent Failure
scenarios.situation: A nightly backup script 'runs' via cron but backups stopped appearing two weeks ago. Nobody noticed until a restore was needed.
choices: Output logging, failure alerting, and restore verification: the job ran silently with errors going nowhere. Every scheduled job needs logged output, alerts on failure, and periodic restore tests.
A faster server.
More disk space.
Better backup software.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats silent scheduled jobs as unmonitored: cron doesn't complain by default. Logging plus alerting plus restore tests is the minimum viable reliability for anything unattended.
scenarios.hint: Who watches a job that can't complain?
evidence: Missing 2 weeks, found during restore need

scenarios.title: The Production Oops
scenarios.situation: A junior admin tests a cleanup loop directly on the production file share 'to save time.' It deletes the wrong directory.
choices: Faster typing.

Echo-first/dry-run development, testing on a copy or single target, confirmations before destructive actions — and never testing untested loops on production. The discipline is procedural, not cleverness.
Better backups only.
Don't let juniors script.
scenarios.why: The correct approach builds safety into the workflow: dry-run first, test small, confirm destructive actions. Backups are the net, not the plan — and 'save time' is how production incidents start.
scenarios.hint: Where should an untested loop run first?
evidence: Wrong directory deleted on prod share

scenarios.title: Clicks vs Code
scenarios.situation: An admin configures cloud resources by clicking, then 'documents' in a wiki. After an outage, nobody can reproduce the environment.
choices: Hire more admins.
Take screenshots of every click.
Wikis are fine — they just need more detail.
Define infrastructure in versioned code: reviewed, reproducible, diffable. Clicks don't scale and wikis rot; code IS the documentation and the recovery plan — re-run to rebuild.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes the environment reproducible: versioned definitions replace tribal clicks, and disaster recovery becomes 're-run the code.' Screenshots and wikis describe; code reproduces.
scenarios.hint: What rebuilds the environment after total loss?

scenarios.title: Run It Twice
scenarios.situation: A deployment script works the first run but corrupts the system on re-run (duplicate entries, double configs).
choices: Deployments should never be retried.
Speed — it should run faster.
Idempotence: safe scripts check state before acting and can run repeatedly without harm. Check-then-act (if not exists, create) makes re-runs safe — essential for retries and scheduled jobs.
The script needs more comments.
scenarios.why: The correct approach designs for re-runs: networks flake, jobs retry, humans re-click. Check-state-before-act makes repetition safe instead of destructive.
scenarios.hint: What happens when the network flakes mid-run and it retries?

scenarios.title: The Mystery Job
scenarios.situation: A server runs a cron job nobody recognizes. It emails a dead address. Nobody dares disable it.
choices: Delete it immediately.
Every scheduled job gets an owner, a purpose comment, and monitored output. Inventory it, find the owner or determine it's safe to retire, then enforce the standard: no orphan jobs.
Forward the emails to someone.
Leave it — it's probably important.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the unknown job as a process failure: jobs need owners and documentation. Investigate before disabling (it might matter), but the standard prevents the next mystery.
scenarios.hint: Why does nobody dare touch it?

domains.description: Stop doing repetitive work by hand: why to automate, scripting basics, scheduling, infrastructure as code, and safe first scripts.

domains.name: Helpdesk Skills

scenarios.title: The Monday Queue
scenarios.situation: Monday 8 AM queue: (a) CEO can't log in, (b) printer jam on floor 3, (c) entire sales floor offline, (d) user wants a new mouse.
choices: c (P1, many down), a (P2, one blocked, high urgency), b (P3, workaround exists), d (P4, request). Impact x urgency — scope of impact sorts first.
b, d, a, c — arrival order.
a, b, c, d — executives first.
d, b, a, c — quick wins first.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sorts by impact x urgency: the sales floor outage dwarfs individual issues, and the CEO's login outranks the printer by urgency. FIFO and title-based ordering both misserve the business.
scenarios.hint: Which issue affects the most work right now?
evidence: CEO login, printer jam, sales floor down, mouse request

scenarios.title: The Useless Ticket
scenarios.situation: Ticket: 'Email broken. Fix ASAP!!!' No user info, no error, no device, no time.
choices: Ignore it until they write better tickets.
Close it — invalid ticket.

Reply with targeted questions (which account, what error exactly, which device, when did it start, can you still log in via web?) and set priority once answered — extract the facts the template needs.
Remote into every machine until you find it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the ticket as raw material: ask the specific questions that complete the picture, in one round, politely. Closing it punishes the user for not knowing your template.
scenarios.hint: What five facts does the template need?

scenarios.title: The Confused Caller
scenarios.situation: A user is lost after a tech said: 'Your GPO isn't applying because the SYSVOL replication is failing on the DC.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you recover the conversation?
choices: Explain what GPO, SYSVOL, and DC mean in detail.
Tell them it's too technical to explain.
Repeat it louder — they weren't listening.

Translate: 'The setting your computer needs isn't arriving — I'm checking the server that sends it now. You don't need to do anything; I'll update you by 2 PM.' No jargon, clear next step, committed time.
scenarios.why: The correct approach translates to impact + action + time: the user needs to know what's happening and when, not the architecture. A jargon lecture serves the tech's ego, not the user.
scenarios.hint: What does the user actually need to know?

scenarios.title: Stuck at L1
scenarios.situation: You've spent 90 minutes on a weird mail-flow issue. You've tried the KB, the usual fixes, and logs show something you've never seen.
choices: Keep grinding — escalation looks bad.
Escalate to L2 with a package: what you tried (with results), the strange log lines, ticket history, user impact — timely escalation with evidence is professional; silent grinding burns the SLA.
Tell the user it's unfixable.
Reboot the mail server and hope.
scenarios.why: The correct approach escalates at the knowledge boundary with evidence: 90 minutes with novel log output is exactly when L2 earns its keep. The package makes the handoff instant instead of a restart.
scenarios.hint: Are you past your access/knowledge boundary?

scenarios.title: The Remote Request
scenarios.situation: 'Hi, this is the CFO — I need you to remote in and fix my laptop right now, here's my cell, call me.' The voice is unfamiliar and the number isn't the CFO's.
choices: Verify identity through a known channel (call the CFO's listed number, check with their assistant) before any remote session — urgency + unfamiliar voice + wrong number is the social-engineering pattern.
Ignore it — CFOs don't call helpdesk.
Remote in immediately — it's the CFO.
Call the number back and help.
scenarios.why: The correct approach verifies before controlling: authority + urgency is the oldest pretext in the book. A 60-second verification call through a known number costs nothing and stops account takeover.
scenarios.hint: What are the tells, and what's the safe verification?
evidence: Claims CFO, unfamiliar voice, unknown callback number

scenarios.title: The Breached SLA
scenarios.situation: A P2 ticket is about to breach its 4-hour SLA. The fix needs a vendor callback that hasn't come.
choices: Close and reopen the ticket to reset the clock.
Let it breach quietly — nothing you can do.
Update the user BEFORE the breach: what's done, what's blocked (vendor), the workaround if any, and the new expectation. Proactive communication preserves trust even when the clock loses.
Change the priority to P3 to avoid the breach.
scenarios.why: The correct approach communicates before the deadline: users forgive delays they were warned about and resent surprises. Gaming priority or the clock corrupts metrics and trust simultaneously.
scenarios.hint: Who should hear about the delay first — and when?

scenarios.title: The Furious User
scenarios.situation: A user is shouting: their presentation starts in 10 minutes and the projector shows 'no signal.' They're blaming IT loudly.
choices: Tell them to calm down.
File a ticket for later.
Argue that it's their cable's fault.

Listen briefly, align ('This is blocking your presentation — let's get it showing'), take ownership, act visibly: check input source, reseat cable, try the laptop — narrate as you go. Calm, fast, specific.
scenarios.why: The correct approach pairs de-escalation with visible action: acknowledgment defuses, narrated troubleshooting rebuilds confidence, and the deadline focuses everyone. Arguing or ticketing abandons them at the worst moment.
scenarios.hint: What's the real deadline here — the fix or the presentation?
evidence: Presentation in 10 min, 'no signal', shouting user

domains.description: The human side of IT: ticketing, SLAs, communicating with non-technical users, escalation, and de-escalation.

domains.name: Professional Skills

scenarios.title: Which Cert First?
scenarios.situation: A helpdesk tech with 1 year experience wants to move toward networking. They ask which certification to pursue.
choices: Skip certs — experience is all that matters.
CISSP — the most prestigious security cert.
Network+: it matches the target lane, builds on their support base, and ladders toward security/cloud next. Study the objectives as a checklist and lab every one — the skill first, the exam second.
Collect all the beginner certs simultaneously.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches the cert to the lane and sequences the ladder: Network+ is the networking on-ramp from support. CISSP needs experience they don't have; cert-hoarding dilutes focus.
scenarios.hint: What lane are they targeting, and what builds toward it?

scenarios.title: The Bus Factor
scenarios.situation: One senior admin 'owns' the backup system entirely in their head. They're going on a 3-week vacation. Management is nervous.
scenarios.prompt: What should have existed, and what's the fix now?
choices: Forbid vacations.
Nothing — they'll be reachable by phone.
Hope nothing breaks.

Runbooks and architecture notes should have existed all along. Now: pair them with a colleague for intensive knowledge transfer, document the restore procedure first (highest risk), then the daily ops. Tribal knowledge is a bus-factor risk, not job security.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats undocumented critical systems as organizational risk: emergency transfer now, documentation culture after. 'Reachable by phone' isn't a continuity plan.
scenarios.hint: What happens if they're unreachable?

scenarios.title: The Friday Deploy
scenarios.situation: An engineer wants to push a firewall change Friday at 4 PM: 'It's small, no backout needed.'
choices: Allow it but watch.
Block it: no backout plan means no change, and Friday 4 PM maximizes blast radius. The change record (what/why/risk/backout/test) is non-negotiable regardless of size.
Do it Monday without paperwork.
Allow it — small changes are safe.
scenarios.why: The correct approach enforces the discipline uniformly: 'small' describes the diff, not the blast radius, and timing is part of risk. The backout plan is the price of admission.
scenarios.hint: What happens if this goes wrong at 4 PM Friday?

scenarios.title: The Technical Screen
scenarios.situation: In an interview: 'Our app is slow for some users. Walk me through your troubleshooting.'
choices: Method, not guesses: clarify scope (which users? when?), reproduce, isolate layers (client/network/server), measure (metrics, not feelings), hypothesize and test, verify the fix. Narrate the method — they're hiring the process.
'I'd Google it.
'I'd reboot the server.'
'It's probably the database.'
scenarios.why: The correct approach demonstrates the troubleshooting method out loud: interviews test how you think under uncertainty, and a structured narrative beats lucky guesses even when the guess is right.
scenarios.hint: Are they testing your answer or your method?
evidence: 'App slow for some users — walk me through it'

scenarios.title: The Snooping Request
scenarios.situation: A manager asks you to quietly read another employee's emails 'to check something.' No HR ticket, no written authorization.
choices: Forward the request to the whole team.
Do it quietly — managers have authority.
Refuse and require proper authorization: email privacy needs HR/legal approval and a documented process. 'Just peek' is a career-ending and potentially illegal favor.
Do it but tell the employee.
scenarios.why: The correct approach holds the line: access without authorization is a policy violation and possibly illegal regardless of who asks. Legitimate investigations come through HR/legal with paperwork.
scenarios.hint: What authorization exists for this access?
evidence: Read employee emails, verbal only, no ticket

scenarios.title: The Comfortable Rut
scenarios.situation: A sysadmin has done the same tasks for 3 years, no new skills, no certs. They're comfortable but worried about stagnation.
choices: Wait for the company to train you.
Stay comfortable — stability is everything.
Quit immediately.

Pick a spike: one lane to go deep in (automation is the highest-leverage for sysadmins), set a cert or project goal with a date, and build visible proof (lab write-ups, scripts shared). Comfort without growth is slow decline.
scenarios.why: The correct approach converts worry into a plan: a chosen spike, a dated goal, and public proof. Waiting for training assigns your career to someone else's budget cycle.
scenarios.hint: What's the smallest committed step with a date?
evidence: 3 yrs same tasks, no new skills

scenarios.title: The Invisible Expert
scenarios.situation: A skilled tech has zero online presence: no GitHub, no write-ups, no community activity. Job applications get no callbacks.
choices: Apply to more jobs.
Publish proof: document one home-lab project publicly (GitHub + write-up), share the process including what broke. Verifiable work beats bullet points — hiring managers click links.
Get another cert first.
Lie on the resume.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes skill verifiable: one public project with honest write-up outperforms another line on a resume. Proof converts applications into conversations.
scenarios.hint: What can a hiring manager verify today?
evidence: Skilled, zero public proof, no callbacks

domains.description: Build the career, not just the skills: paths, certifications, documentation, change management, and your professional brand.

lessons.title: Adaptive Learning Foundations - Core concepts
concepts: Mastery learning (Bloom): advancement depends on reaching roughly 80-90% mastery, not on the calendar. Time becomes the variable; learning is the constant.

Knowledge Space Theory (Doignon and Falmagne) formalizes prerequisites: a learner's knowledge state is the set of mastered items, and only items whose prerequisites are all mastered sit on the learnable 'fringe'. Adaptive systems assess by navigating this structure.
Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development: target tasks just beyond what the learner can do alone, with scaffolding that fades. Too easy bores; too hard frustrates - adaptivity lives in the gap.
Item Response Theory powers computerized adaptive testing: each response updates the ability estimate, and the next item is chosen at that level - converging in far fewer questions than a fixed form.
Retrieval practice and spacing beat re-reading and cramming: testing strengthens memory, and spaced intervals exploit the spacing effect. Schedule reassessments, not just lessons.
Close the loop fast: assess, diagnose the missing prerequisite, remediate, reassess. The unit of adaptation is the knowledge state, not the test score.

example.code:
prereq = {"fractions": set(),
          "decimals": {"fractions"},
          "percents": {"decimals", "fractions"}}
mastered = {"fractions", "decimals"}
fringe = [item for item, ps in prereq.items()
          if item not in mastered and ps <= mastered]
print("learnable next:", fringe)
example.walkthrough: The fringe is every unmastered item whose prerequisites are all mastered - here, percents. An adaptive system offers exactly this set next, never items the learner is not ready for and never ones already known.

pitfalls: Common trap: optimizing the test score instead of the knowledge state - scores can be gamed; prerequisite structure cannot.
Common trap: one fixed curriculum for everyone - prior-knowledge variance makes linear paths wasteful for half the class.
Common trap: placing once and never reassessing - knowledge states shift; forgetting is real and measurable.
Common trap: reading engagement dashboards as learning - clicks and time-on-page do not equal mastery.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Adaptive Foundations move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Adaptive Learning Foundations
concepts: Adaptive Learning Foundations is a multi-step process within Adaptive Learning Foundations: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Adaptive Learning Foundations to the broader Adaptive Learning Foundations ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Adaptive Learning Foundations begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Adaptive Learning Foundations. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Adaptive Learning Foundations as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Adaptive Learning Foundations flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it top to bottom: each domain builds on the previous one, and later scenarios assume earlier knowledge
Every lesson ends with a knowledge check: answer correctly and the lesson auto-completes. Wrong answers send you back to review — this is verification, not clicking through
Scenarios are timed decision exercises with evidence to examine. Treat each like the real thing: read everything, decide, then commit
Your progress saves automatically. Domains unlock as you complete prerequisites — the path guides you, but you set the pace

example.code:
LEARN path: lessons -> scenarios -> labs -> drills
TERMINAL: hands-on command practice
MOCK: full timed assessment when ready

Suggested daily loop:
  1. Complete 2-3 lessons (with knowledge checks)
  2. Work 3-5 scenarios in those domains
  3. Run 1 lab end-to-end
  4. 10 minutes of drills
example.walkthrough: The bootcamp mirrors how professionals actually work: learn the concept, apply it under realistic conditions, then prove it in the lab. Skipping straight to the mock without the lessons is the fastest way to fail it.

pitfalls: Skipping lessons and jumping to scenarios — the scenarios assume lesson knowledge
Treating the knowledge check as a formality instead of a real self-test
Ignoring the terminal and labs — hands-on reps are where durable skill comes from
lessons.try_it: Open the Learn path and complete the first lesson's knowledge check to see auto-completion in action.

lessons.title: assessment Strategy: How to Win
concepts: The assessment rewards applied understanding over memorization — every domain here maps to something you will actually be asked to do
Time management wins: in timed assessments, bank the easy wins first, flag the hard ones, and never leave a question blank
Wrong answers are data: each missed scenario reveals a specific gap. Log it, revisit the lesson, and re-attempt until the pattern clicks
Sleep and spacing beat cramming: 90-minute focused sessions with breaks outperform marathon sessions, especially the week before assessment day

example.code:
The 3-pass method for timed assessments:
  Pass 1 (40% of time): answer everything you know cold
  Pass 2 (40% of time): work the flagged mediums with evidence
  Pass 3 (20% of time): educated guesses on the rest

Never spend 10 minutes on one question while five easy ones wait.
example.walkthrough: Elimination is a skill: practice ruling out two wrong choices fast, then deciding between the final two. Most scenario questions are designed so two options are clearly wrong to a prepared candidate.

pitfalls: Changing answers without new evidence — your first instinct after study is usually right
Perfectionism on one hard question while easy points expire
Studying new material the night before instead of reviewing what you know
lessons.try_it: Do one full timed mock this week using the 3-pass method, even before you feel ready. Baseline yourself.

lessons.title: Course Map: What You Will Master
concepts: This bootcamp has 15+ domains covering the full Adaptive Foundations landscape — from foundations to the capstone project
Core domains teach the must-know systems; the Systems Anatomy domain teaches you to see them as living, connected flows
The capstone project proves you can build and operate a real system end-to-end — this is your interview story
The mock assessment simulates the real assessment so there are no surprises on the day

example.code:
Adaptive Foundations mastery map:
  Foundations -> Core systems (domains 2-10)
  -> Systems Anatomy (see it all connected)
  -> Capstone (build it yourself)
  -> Mock (prove it under pressure)
example.walkthrough: Start with: Study Systems. It unlocks everything downstream — the path is sequential for a reason.

pitfalls: Treating all domains as equal — weight your time toward the heaviest-tested areas
Skipping Systems Anatomy — it is the differentiator between passing and excelling
Saving the capstone for 'later' — start it early, iterate as you learn
lessons.try_it: Skim the domain list in the Learn path and note which three domains matter most for your goal. Start there after Start Here.

lessons.title: Data, Information, and the IPO Model
concepts: Data is raw facts; information is data processed to answer a question — IT turns the first into the second
IPO (Input -> Process -> Output) describes every system and every troubleshooting flow: find the failing stage first
Digital data is discrete: everything reduces to bits, so storage, memory, and bandwidth use powers of two
Garbage in, garbage out: output quality can never exceed input quality plus process correctness

example.code:
Troubleshooting with IPO:
  INPUT broken? cable, keyboard, sensor, user entry
  PROCESS broken? CPU pegged, app crashed, logic bug
  OUTPUT broken? display, printer, network send
Ask 'which stage fails?' before touching anything.
example.walkthrough: IPO is a diagnostic lens: 'it doesn't work' is not a diagnosis — the stage is.

pitfalls: Treating symptoms as the problem — 'slow computer' is output; find the stage
Forgetting the human is part of input — mistyped data breaks perfect systems
Assuming digital means exact — sensors, rounding, and encoding all lose fidelity
lessons.try_it: Take one broken thing near you and label the failing IPO stage with one sentence of evidence.

lessons.title: How Computers Represent Everything in Binary
concepts: A bit is one binary digit; 8 bits make a byte — the smallest addressable unit, one ASCII character
Binary counting doubles per position (1,2,4,8,16...): 1011 = 8+2+1 = 11 decimal
Hex is compressed binary (1 hex digit = 4 bits) — MACs, memory dumps, color codes
Storage uses decimal GB (marketing) vs binary GiB (OS): a '500 GB' drive shows ~465 GB — units differ, nothing is missing

example.walkthrough: Memorize 2^10=1024 (K), 2^20 (M), 2^30 (G) — they recur in addressing, subnetting, storage.

pitfalls: Mixing decimal GB with binary GiB — the 'missing space' is math, not theft
Thinking hex is advanced — it is just shorthand for binary
Forgetting Unicode — ASCII's 128 chars can't hold the world's languages; UTF-8 is the default
lessons.try_it: Convert your birth year to binary and hex by hand, then verify with a calculator.

lessons.title: Hardware Meets Software: The Big Picture
concepts: CPU executes; RAM holds working data at nanosecond speed; storage persists without power but far slower — performance is the triangle between them
The OS is the resource broker: scheduling CPU, managing memory, arbitrating hardware so apps don't fight
Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) wakes the machine and hands control to the OS bootloader
Apps never touch hardware directly on modern systems — every request goes through the OS

example.code:
Why RAM helps a slow PC:
  RAM full -> OS pages to disk (slow)
  More RAM -> less paging -> CPU stops waiting
But if CPU sits at 100%, RAM won't help —
diagnose the bottleneck before buying the fix.
example.walkthrough: Every performance problem is a bottleneck hunt: find the saturated resource and the fix names itself.

pitfalls: Upgrading the wrong component — measure first with Task Manager/top
Calling the OS 'the computer' — it is one layer in the stack
Ignoring firmware — unpatched UEFI is a real attack surface
lessons.try_it: Open Task Manager (or top) and name the busiest resource and top process right now.

lessons.title: Types of Software and Licensing
concepts: System software (OS, drivers) manages hardware; applications do user work; utilities (AV, backup) maintain the system
Proprietary software is licensed, not sold — audits and compliance are real in business
Open source ships with source under licenses (MIT, GPL) granting use/modification with conditions
SaaS turned software into metered subscriptions — licensing is now identity-based

example.code:
Before installing on company hardware:
  1. Which license? (proprietary/OSS/SaaS)
  2. Seats/devices allowed? 3. Transferable?
  4. Expiry/renewal date?
Answer all four first.
example.walkthrough: Unlicensed software is a legal AND security liability — cracked installers are classic malware droppers.

pitfalls: Installing 'free' paid software at work — piracy with extra steps
Ignoring GPL obligations when shipping products built on GPL code
SaaS seat sprawl — ex-employees with active logins invite breaches
lessons.try_it: List your paid apps and check one license term you've never read.

lessons.title: Files, Formats, and Compatibility
concepts: A file extension (.docx, .pdf, .png) is a hint about format — the bytes inside determine what it really is
